result_text:
**Recommendation: do not expand on this evidence, and do not book any responder-hour savings.** The data does not show that Assist sped up recovery. With a single cutover and no holdout, it can't establish cause in either direction.

**What I found (420 incidents, Jun 1–14):**
- **The headline gain isn't distinguishable from zero.** The median time to close fell 1.8 hours (7.27 to 5.44), but the 95% bootstrap interval runs from −2.2 to +1.7 hours, so it includes no change. The mean time to close rose slightly (7.1 to 7.5 hours). Mean responder minutes were flat (90.2 vs 90.9), so the credible responder-hour saving is about zero.
- **The median fell because the incident mix changed.** Volume stayed at 15 per group per day, but sev1 incidents dropped from 28 to 14 and sev3 rose from 98 to 154. Sev1 went from exactly 4 a day to exactly 2 from Jun 8. I can't tell from these files whether Assist changed how incidents are labeled or whether the incidents really got easier.
- **Within every severity level, Assist incidents were slower and took more responder time.** The table shows Assist minus manual medians, with 95% intervals:

  | Severity | Time to close (hours) | Responder minutes |
  |---|---|---|
  | Sev1 | +9.3 (7.7 to 12.0) | +69 (55 to 89) |
  | Sev2 | +3.8 (3.0 to 4.3) | +40 (30 to 47.5) |
  | Sev3 | +2.25 (1.9 to 2.5) | +26 (24 to 29) |

  This is consistent with the responders who say Assist adds work on difficult incidents. If severity itself was changed by Assist, this by-severity view could be misleading too, so I'm not claiming Assist made things slower either.
- **Staffing changed on the same day.** Active responders rose by 2 in each group (12 to 14 and 11 to 13) on Jun 8, with scheduled hours up roughly 20%. That is a second change that could have affected recovery.
- **Close records are missing, mostly for Assist.** 11 incidents have no close record: 10 in the Assist week and 1 in the manual week. Five of the 14 Assist sev1 incidents are among them. The files don't say whether those are still open, unrecorded or lost in the export, so I can't say which way this skews the result. Even counting them all as the slowest incidents, the raw median still favors Assist, but the sev1 comparison rests on only 9 closed Assist incidents.

**What the data can't establish:**
- Any causal effect of Assist, because the week before is not a valid control. The staffing change, the severity shift and ordinary week-to-week variation all moved at the same time.
- Why sev1 volume halved.
- Whether the missing close records change the picture.

**Before deciding on expansion:**
- Ask the service owners and the Assist team whether severity is set or changed after Assist touches an incident.
- Find out what the 11 incidents without close records actually are.
- Run a staggered rollout or a holdout across the remaining groups. The `causal-identification-review` and `decision-analysis` skills could help design that and weigh the decision.

The working ledger is `ledger.md` in the work directory (`/var/folders/4_/s6fbcjyn4b13xdxkd3lv0kw00000gn/T/arm-s15-pre-2-j4pol9wj/work`). The record validator passed on it (exit 0), which only confirms the file's structure, not that the analysis is right.
